newsitem.title: INDIA: Oman says gas pipeline with India not possible now.
newsitem.headline: Oman says gas pipeline with India not possible now.

text.p: Oman said on Thursday an ambitious subsea natural gas pipeline project linking Oman and India did not look possible at present due to technical problems and lack of adequate gas reserves.

"Today if you ask me I would say no," Omani Commerce and Industry Minister Makboul Ali Bin Sultan told a news conference. He was accompanying Oman's Sultan Qaboos Bin Said on his four-day India visit.
Makboul said a joint committee of experts was looking into the project's feasibility.
"I hope when the committee meets and looks at all the other angles and points in the study they may find out that it is feasible. Today it is not."
"Today if you ask me if I am an optimist or pessimist I would say I am pessimist," Makboul said, adding that the study was expected to be completed by July.
Makboul said an earlier study had shown that the Oman's reserves of gas were very small compared to that of various other countries.
"It is true, if you ask me today if Oman has enough gas for the project. No," he said.
Makboul said a technical study on the project did not provide full answers and the economic study was based on the assumption that many investors would come in.
But it was found the Oman government must bear the entire burden of $10 billion on the project, he said.
"I hope it will happen but I am not very optimistic," Makboul earlier told a meeting of the Federation of Indian Commerce and Industry.
He said the Gulf state has spent $70 million to $80 million on the feasibility study for the project.
India said on Wednesday the project had been put on hold in the absence of proper technology.
"For the time being...we are keeping it in abeyance until the technology is available," Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral told reporters.
India and Oman signed a memorandum of understanding in 1993 to build a pipeline between the two nations under the Arabian Sea.
According to the original plan, the proposed pipeline would be more than 1,300 km (813 miles) long and lie up to two miles under the ocean's surface.
Makboul also said it had been decided to set up a joint investment company with $100 million in capital to promote investments in the two countries.
He said the company would have equal shareholding by Omani and Indian private entrepreneurs.
Makboul said Oman was in favour of a preferential trading arrangment with India since this would benefit both countries.
India and Oman on Wednesday signed several agreements to boost bilateral cooperation, including one on forming a joint venture company for a $1.1 billion fertiliser complex in the gulf nation.

Qaboos, on the third day of his visit, the first to a South Asian country, on Thursday exchanged views with Gujral and the Civil Aviation Minister C. M. Ibrahim. The Sultan is due to leave for home early on Friday.
